I truly feel that competitive fighting games have the hardest time on PC than other platforms. (The rest is a rant. Read at your own risk.)

First off, to be "competitive", they must have complete parity between platforms. The XBone and PS4 versions should run at the same framerate, with the same feel for the controls (no platform should feel like they have "input lag" against the other) so that during competitions, any player can play on any platform without using the platform as an excuse. There are more areas for parity, but those are two simple ones.

At the same time, the "PC Master Race" mentality causes trouble with those needs for full parity. Users are reporting that the resolution is less than 1080p, and locked at 60 FPS max, with the game speed tied to framerate. This decision was probably made for parity across all three platforms. The consoles were probably only capable of running the game at 60 FPS at 720P, so that was the standard they decided on. While this goes against the "PC Master Race" attitude, it makes the PC version equal to the console versions, for competitive play. (You may also notice that there is PC/PS4 cross-competitive play online. Also proof that decisions were made for parity)

Not including DirectInput, causing PS4 arcade sticks to not work, on launch is a separate mistake that they seem to plan on resolving, but it's another black mark separate from my argument.

It seems that the only two options for fighting games are to dissappoint the PC Master Race, or to sacrifice parity, damaging the competitiveness of their game. The third option is for the PC platform to stop getting competitive fighters altogether, which I don't think anyone wants. I feel that this is a lose-lose situation, with there always being a group who is unhappy with the game.

(One major issue that could result in the PC release being the platform that competitive players practice on is that the gameplay is [reportedly] locked to the framerate. Anyone with a beefy enough computer could force the game to run at a higher framerate, causing the gameplay to be quicker. Practicing at 75 FPS would increase gameplay by 25%, making gameplay at 60 FPS feel slower, giving them an edge during tournaments. If Capcom stopped the practice of locking gameplay to framerate, they could at least unlock the framerate on PC, helping the PC Master Race people, and preventing people with a certain platform from have an edge during practice.)
An FPS lock on a fighting game though is rather needed for it to be seriously competitive. Reactions must be timed down to a couple frames and each animation having a set number.

Allow me to play devil's advocate a little: What if all character animations were created for 60 FPS, but the backgrounds were unlocked? If a character's model had 3 frames of "wind up" animation for an action, those three frames could be extended over 6 frames of 120 FPS gameplay, resulting in the same number of milliseconds of reaction time, but still supplying a higher framerate for those that look for that.

I am not personally good at fighting games, but understand the need for an even playing field for competitive play. I honestly want to hear why that may not be as good an idea as I would think.
Simple fix would be to keep the FPS lock but allow for better resolutions.

Why are there so many bad PC ports in these days?

Personal theory: game publishers don't want to make games for PC. They're stuck between not wanting to leave money on the table and wanting to push gamers all into consoles. Why? Static-hardware platforms are much easier to target in code and debug, developers aren't competing with general purpose computer software developers and makes it possible to suppress salaries, consoles have substantial DRM and anti-piracy mechanisms, no modding (GTA:SA shows a worst case scenario), no need to give away super high quality assets consoles can't render but PCMR folks with $3K graphics cards demand.

The idea is to get current PC gamers to think "well, maybe I'll just get this one on console" to get that box in the house, and then each release after that becomes a question of which platform they'll get it on, with the hopes they'll choose the console.

I don't think it's just that. Console games are also increasingly broken even though the developers can test their games on the exact hardware everybody will be playing their title on. I think a big part of the problem is that from the late 90s to earlyish 2000s the video game industry was a major destination for skilled talent. For instance some absurd chunk of 30 something programmers today are going to have had John Carmack as an influence to some degree. Now a days who wants to go work for EA, Capcom, Ubisoft or other big name publisher/devs? Terrible working conditions, terrible pay, terrible benefits, minimal creative input, and if your life dream is to make video games you can actually do that completely independently now a days thanks to Steam. Now a days there's also far more interesting destinations for highly skilled developers from SpaceX to AI startups to Google. The net result has been brain drain of talent away from the console-centric AAA game industry at the same time that games themselves are becoming increasingly technically complex. It's a recipe for failure.
